title: it can stop
hookLine: it can stop; not a heaven you go to, a fire with nothing left to burn
last: TANHA — THE WANTING IS THE WOBBLE.

cards: A headache that's sat behind the eyes all afternoon finally lifts. Nobody marked the minute it arrived. Sometimes the leaving is the only part anyone notices.
If the Buddha's teaching stopped at the first two truths, a diagnosis and a cause, it would be a heavy teaching. It doesn't stop there.
The third truth says the wobble can end, and the word for that ending is one you've likely heard: as the name of a band, a kind of heaven, a perfect afternoon. It's none of those.

teach.b: The third noble truth is nirodha. Cessation. Stopping.
In the first sermon it's put simply: when the thirst fades away completely, when it's let go and released, dukkha ends. Remove the cause, and what it causes stops.
The name for that ending is nirvana, in Sanskrit, or nibbana, in Pali.
Teachers link the word to a flame going out, the way a lamp goes out when there's no more fuel. That's the image. Not a place you go.
The fire of craving, with nothing left to burn. People sometimes hear that and think it sounds like nothingness. The texts don't describe it that way.

The Dhammapada lists the best things there are: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentment the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." Happiness. Not blankness.
And there's an exchange in the discourses that uses the same fire. A wanderer asks the Buddha where a fully awakened person goes after death.

teach.h: WHICH WAY DID THE FIRE GO?
teach.b: The Buddha asks him: when a fire goes out in front of you, which direction did it go? North? South?
The man admits the question doesn't fit. The fire just went out.
The Buddha says this question is like that one. Buddhist traditions describe nirvana in different words, and the texts often say what it isn't. But the third truth itself is simple.
The wobble is real. And it isn't permanent.

how: Buddhists speak of nirvana as the end of craving and of dukkha; in Theravada it is the goal of the path, and Mahayana traditions describe awakening in their own terms, while everyday practice keeps attention on letting go.

games.q: what's inside the truth — tap the pairs.
p: which way did the fire go?

s: the Dhammapada calls it "the highest happiness."
nirvana's image is a flame going out
the fire of craving with nothing left to burn.
the Buddha said exactly where an awakened person goes after death
he answered with a question: when a fire goes out, which way did it go?

games.q: a wanderer asks the Buddha where a fully awakened person goes after death. what does the Buddha do?
o: says they go nowhere at all.
asks which direction a fire goes when it goes out.
games.why: he asks about the fire. north, south, east, west? the question doesn't fit, and the Buddha says the wanderer's question is like that one.

practice: The bell gives you about forty-five seconds. Notice any small wanting that's here. Then any small ache.
Then look for a moment, even a flicker, where neither is pulling at you. A gap. A small quiet between two thoughts.
It might be tiny. When it closes, wait for the next one. That tiny thing is what the third truth is pointing at.

wordCard.voice: Nirvana. The third truth's word: when the thirst ends, dukkha ends. The flame with nothing left to burn. Tenth word.

orig.note: Pali: nibbāna, the going out of a flame. Sanskrit: nirvāṇa. The third noble truth is nirodha, cessation.

carryVoice: Your line: there is an end. Not a place to get to; a fire that's gone out. See you tomorrow.

sources.q: Health is the greatest of gifts, contentment the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness.
